THE ROMANOVS 1613–1918
745pp. Weidenfeld and Nicolson. £25 (US $35).
Simon Sebag Montefiore
In The Romanovs , Simon Sebag Montefiore sticks to a method that has served him well in the past: he looks closely at the inner chambers of supreme power in Russia. But the book’s scale makes it a rather different enterprise from his earlier studies of Catherine the Great’s relationship with Potemkin and of Stalin’s “court”. Here the ethnographic detail has to be maintained over a whole dynasty, three centuries, twenty rulers and an exhausting cast of relatives and hangers-on. Sebag Montefiore carries out this task with enviable stamina and unrelenting vim. His account has the gossipy charm that readers will recognize from his earlier work – an ease of manner that artfully

...

by Sebag Montefiore, Simon, 1965- author
Publication date 2017 Topics Romanov, House of , Dynastie des Romanov , Kings and rulers , Russia -- Kings and rulers -- Biography , Russia -- History -- 1613-1917 , Russie -- Histoire -- 1613-1917 , Russia Publisher New York : Vintage Books, A division of Penguin Random House LLC Collection internetarchivebooks ; printdisabled Contributor Internet Archive Language English Item Size 2.4G
xxxiv, 748 pages, 32 unnumbered pages of plates : 23 cm
The Romanovs were the most successful dynasty of modern times, ruling a sixth of the world's surface for three centuries. How did one family turn a war-ruined principality into the world's greatest empire? And how did they lose it all? This is the intimate story of twenty tsars and tsarinas, some touched by genius, some by madness, but all inspired by holy autocracy and imperial ambition. Simon Sebag Montefiore's chronicle reveals their secret world of unlimited power and ruthless empire-building, overshadowed by palace conspiracy, family rivalries, sexual decadence and wild extravagance. Drawing on new archival research, Montefiore delivers an enthralling epic of triumph and tragedy, love and murder, that is both a universal study of power and a portrait of empire that helps define Russia today.--Page [4] of cover
